questions.question: Explain the causes, terms and effects of the Natives Land Act of 1913.
questions.expected_answer: Many Africans farmed outside the reserves as landowners, rent-paying tenants, labour tenants or sharecroppers who used their own oxen and equipment and gave half the harvest to the landowner; in the Orange Free State African sharecroppers were often successful. White farmers wanted Africans as labourers rather than competitors, mine owners wanted migrant labour from the reserves, and segregationists wanted separate areas. Act 27 of 1913, in force from 19 June 1913, reserved scheduled areas of about 7 per cent of the land for Africans, banned them from buying or renting land from non-Africans outside these areas and outlawed sharecropping in the Orange Free State, allowing Africans on white farms only as labourers or labour tenants; the Cape was treated differently because of the franchise. Thousands of families were evicted in winter, losing livestock, the reserves became overcrowded and more men became migrant workers. The Act was the foundation of land segregation, and land restitution today uses 19 June 1913 as its starting date.

questions.question: Explain what satyagraha was and describe the campaign of 1913 to 1914.
questions.expected_answer: Satyagraha, Gandhi's term meaning truth-force, was non-violent resistance: deliberately and openly breaking unjust laws and accepting arrest and imprisonment, to expose injustice. It began in 1906 against the Transvaal registration law, and in 1908 Indians burned their certificates outside the Hamidia Mosque. In 1913 the grievances were the annual three-pound tax on Indians who stayed in Natal after indenture, the Searle judgment which declared Hindu and Muslim marriages invalid, and the Immigrants Regulation Act restricting movement. Women crossed provincial borders without permits and encouraged Newcastle coal miners to strike in October 1913. On 6 November 1913 about two thousand marchers crossed from Charlestown into the Transvaal at Volksrust; Gandhi was arrested and strikes spread to the Natal sugar estates, with strikers shot in clashes. Protest in India and Britain led to the Gandhi-Smuts agreement and the Indian Relief Act of 1914, which abolished the tax and recognised Indian marriages.

questions.question: Compare the responses to the Land Act and to anti-Indian laws in 1913 and explain why their results differed.
questions.expected_answer: Both were responses to Union laws discriminating by race. The SANNC opposed the Land Act with petitions, deputations and a delegation to London in 1914, and Plaatje wrote Native Life in South Africa, but the British government refused to intervene and the Act remained. The Indian community used satyagraha, mass non-violent law-breaking, strikes by coal and sugar workers and the march of November 1913, and won the Indian Relief Act of 1914. The Indian campaign succeeded partly because mass strikes disrupted the economy, because arrests and shootings caused outrage in India and Britain, and because the British government of India pressed South Africa, while the demands were limited and did not threaten white control of land. The Land Act served core interests of white farmers and the mines, so the government would not change it. Even so, Indian gains were limited, as Indians remained without the vote and faced discrimination, and later movements such as the 1952 Defiance Campaign learned from satyagraha.
